cards.claim: The paper identifies that iterative harness evolution using finite feedback creates an adaptive overfitting risk where performance on the evolve set does not generalize to unseen tasks.
cards.evidence_quote: test-time harness evolution repeatedly proposes and selects edits using feedback from a finite evolve set, creating an adaptive overfitting risk: evolve-set performance may improve without corresponding gains on unseen tasks.

cards.claim: The authors propose RRSI, a framework that regularizes both the proposal and selection of harness edits to prevent retention of improvements driven by benchmark-specific signals or noise.
cards.evidence_quote: RRSI regularizes both sides of the evolution loop: it encourages simpler and more reusable edits when proposing candidates, and applies robust selection criteria to avoid retaining improvements driven by benchmark-specific signals, evaluation noise, or unnecessary complexity.

cards.claim: Experiments on eight benchmarks show RRSI improves held-out splits by up to 4.7 points out of distribution while using fewer policy tokens than unregularized evolution.
cards.evidence_quote: it gains up to 14.1 points on the evolving split and improves all six held-out splits, by up to 4.7 points out of distribution, on fewer policy tokens than unregularized evolution spends.

cards.claim: The paper identifies that overfitting arises from encoding benchmark-specific patterns, promoting candidates favored by evaluation noise, and accumulating complexity without improving the underlying agent mechanism.
cards.evidence_quote: The evolution search may encode benchmark-specific patterns, promote candidates favored by the evaluation noise, or accumulate complexity that improves evolve-set scores without improving the underlying agent mechanism.

cards.claim: The paper defines an agent as a combination of a backbone policy and a harness that manages system prompts, control flow, tools, and memory.
cards.evidence_quote: We consider an agent 𝐴= (𝜋, 𝐻) built from a backbone policy 𝜋and a harness 𝐻. The harness is everything around the weights...: the system and task prompts, the control flow that decides when the agent plans, acts, reflects or stops, the tool interfaces and their descriptions, the memory and skill files the agent may consult, and the context management that decides what the policy sees at each step.

cards.claim: The authors define task performance as the expected score of trajectories on a task set and token cost as the expected number of tokens consumed.
cards.evidence_quote: For a task set D, we measure task performance and policy-token cost as 𝑆(𝐻; D) = 𝔼𝑥∼D 𝔼𝜏∼𝐴(·|𝑥) [𝑟(𝑥, 𝜏)], 𝐶(𝐻; D) = 𝔼𝑥∼D 𝔼𝜏∼𝐴(·|𝑥) [𝑐(𝜏)], where 𝑐(𝜏) is the number of policy tokens consumed by the trajectory.

cards.claim: The paper identifies that harness evolution typically treats the harness as the optimization variable while keeping the backbone policy fixed.
cards.evidence_quote: Harness evolution treats 𝐻as the optimization variable while keeping the backbone policy fixed (Lee et al., 2026b).

cards.claim: The authors claim that their proposed RRSI method regularizes how the evolution moves through the search space to prevent leakage and noise.
cards.evidence_quote: RRSI follows this recursive improvement process and keeps the harness edit space open, but regularizes how the evolution moves through that space. The key idea is to translate regularization principles from machine learning into an adaptive harness search: sparse updates limit how many mechanisms can change in response to one round of feedback, evidence-aware credit assignment prevents the search from repeatedly spending its capacity on hypotheses it has already falsified, and conservative selection prevents leakage, evaluation noise, or unjustified resource growth from becoming permanent harness state.

cards.claim: RRSI regularizes the proposal distribution by annealing update capacity, using evidence-aware credit assignment, and structuring exploration.
cards.evidence_quote: RRSI regularizes it in three ways: it anneals how much update capacity a single round may exercise, it makes credit assignment evidence-aware over the whole run, and it structures where that capacity is spent.

cards.claim: RRSI employs leakage screening to reject candidates that explicitly encode task-specific values or answers before full evaluation.
cards.evidence_quote: Before full evaluation, a critic reads each candidate diff and rejects edits that explicitly encode task names, entity names, task-specific values, answers, or other logic specific to the evolve benchmark

cards.claim: The approach uses stability-aware acceptance with a noise-adjusted floor to prevent selecting candidates due to stochastic variation.
cards.evidence_quote: A candidate must satisfy the noise-adjusted floor ˆS(H′) ≥ S★−δ. The floor prevents the search from walking downhill through a sequence of regressions that are individually small enough to be mistaken for noise.

cards.claim: RRSI uses L1-style structural pruning to sparsify the retained harness by deleting unproductive components.
cards.evidence_quote: The annealed budget in Equation (4) sparsifies each update; pruning sparsifies the retained harness. RRSI tracks whether recently exercised components have produced a strictly positive measured gain over a fixed pruning window.

cards.claim: Components that remain unproductive are reported as deletion targets to make the harness structurally sparser.
cards.evidence_quote: Components that remain unproductive are reported to the proposer as deletion targets in subsequent rounds. This process imitates the Lasso/L1-style sparsification: mechanisms with insufficient evidence of utility are removed entirely, so the retained harness becomes structurally sparser rather than merely cheaper in aggregate.

cards.claim: The pruning rule deletes discrete harness components based on observed contribution, unlike Lasso which reduces parameters through regularization.
cards.evidence_quote: The correspondence is again qualitative, i.e., Lasso reduces the number of parameters through L1 regularization, whereas our pruning rule deletes discrete harness components based on their observed contribution.

cards.claim: RRSI improves performance on all held-out splits across coding, agentic workspace, and engineering design domains compared to the base harness.
cards.evidence_quote: RRSI improves every split outside the evolve set, in all three domains.

cards.claim: The method achieves specific point gains on in-distribution held-out tasks such as 2.3 points on Harvey LAB and 1.8 points on SWE-bench Verified.
cards.evidence_quote: SWE-bench Verified gains 1.8 points although repository-level bug fixing was never scored. The in-distribution held-out split of Harvey LAB gains 2.3

cards.claim: RRSI outperforms baselines on out-of-distribution benchmarks, where the ranking of prior methods inverts compared to their performance on the evolve set.
cards.evidence_quote: The separation appears out of distribution, and there the ranking inverts. Meta-Harness, the strongest baseline on the evolve split, adds 0.9 points to the out-of-distribution average

cards.claim: The performance gains are not artifacts of judge-mediated grading because engineering design tasks are graded by deterministic simulations.
cards.evidence_quote: each EngDesign and Frontier-Eng task is graded by its own simulation or testbench, the grading is deterministic, and a design either meets the stated constraints or does not.

cards.claim: Removing acceptance constraints increases the evolve-set score but decreases out-of-distribution transfer and increases token cost, indicating that unconstrained selection accepts noise.
cards.evidence_quote: Without the acceptance constraints the evolve-set score rises from 90.5 to 91.5 while the out-of-distribution average falls from 43.6 to 41.0 and token cost rises by half

cards.claim: RRSI improves performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and transfers gains to SWE-bench Verified when using both Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8 policies.
cards.evidence_quote: As shown in Table 3, under Gemini 3.5 Flash, RRSI improves Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 64.6 to 78.7 and transfers a 2.2-point gain to SWE-bench Verified.

cards.claim: The evolved harness improves performance on an unseen, weaker backbone (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite), demonstrating that the benefits are not specific to the search policy.
cards.evidence_quote: As shown in Table 4, Terminal-Bench 2.1 accuracy rises from 11.2 to 14.6, a 30.4% relative gain against a base score less than a fifth of the search policy’s.

cards.claim: No evolved harness is as cheap as H0, which costs 1.56 million tokens and 21.2 steps.
cards.evidence_quote: No evolved harness is as cheap as 𝐻0, at 1.56 million tokens and 21.2 steps

cards.claim: Evolution buys part of its gain with test-time compute, where the budget decides how much.
cards.evidence_quote: evolution does buy part of its gain with test-time compute; the budget decides how much.

cards.claim: The authors propose regularizing search dynamics by assigning credit over full history, filtering task-specific logic before scoring, and using a noise-adjusted baseline.
cards.evidence_quote: We keep the same open edit space and instead regularize the search dynamics: credit assigned over the full evolution history, task-specific logic filtered before scoring, and acceptance against a noise-adjusted baseline

cards.claim: Existing approaches to automating harness evolution rely on benchmark scores without terms for generalization, leading to gains that often do not survive changes in the evaluation suite.
cards.evidence_quote: Throughout, the search is driven by the score on the suite it optimizes against, with no term for generalization, and the cost is not hypothetical: reported gains often do not survive a change of suite

cards.claim: A well-designed agent harness can substitute for model scale, recovering much of a larger backbone's capability at a fraction of the cost.
cards.evidence_quote: A well-designed harness can even substitute for scale, recovering much of a larger backbone’s capability at a fraction of the cost

cards.claim: The engineering of agent harnesses is overwhelmingly manual and incurs recurring costs with every new model release.
cards.evidence_quote: This engineering is overwhelmingly manual, and because the best harness is tied to a specific backbone, its cost is paid again with every model release

cards.claim: RRSI improves held-out and cross-benchmark performance while using less inference cost than unregularized evolution.
cards.evidence_quote: Across coding, agentic workspace, and engineering design tasks, the resulting harnesses improve held-out and cross-benchmark performance while using less inference cost than unregularized evolution.

cards.claim: The paper proposes RRSI to address apparent self-improvement that reflects benchmark-specific fitting or evaluation noise rather than transferable progress.
cards.evidence_quote: RRSI addresses this problem by regularizing both proposal and selection while leaving the harness edit space open.

cards.claim: The study is limited to harness-level recursive self-improvement with frozen backbone models, excluding settings where model weights are updated.
cards.evidence_quote: Our study focuses on harness-level recursive self-improvement with frozen backbone models, and therefore does not address settings where model weights are updated during evolution.

cards.claim: The effectiveness of RRSI may depend on the quality of the feedback signal and the chosen search budget because it relies on a finite evolve set.
cards.evidence_quote: In addition, RRSI still relies on a finite evolve set and several regularization hyperparameters, so its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the feedback signal and the chosen search budget.

rejected.claim: The method uses L0-style annealed update sparsity to cap the number of independently attributable edits in a proposal.
rejected.evidence_quote: We therefore cap the number of independently attributable edits that may be included in one proposal. At round t of a T-round run, this budget is bt = l bmin + (bmax −bmin) · 1/2(1 + cos(πt/T))m.

rejected.claim: RRSI produces the lightest harness among compared methods, dominating others in cost and out-of-distribution performance due to its L1-style budget and pruning rule.
rejected.evidence_quote: Figure 4 (a) shows the consequence: all four sit in the region RRSI dominates, spending more policy tokens per trial for a lower out-of-distribution average.
